# MEMORANDUM

**TO:** Supervising Partner
**FROM:** [Associate]
**RE:** Project Curd: Lepund Creamery Holdings, Inc. purchase of Kettlebrook Organic Creamery, Inc.: issues review of transaction documents
**DATE:** November 18, 2026
**PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL | ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT**

---

## I. Summary

I reviewed all eight documents in the folder:

1. the Stock Purchase Agreement dated November 6, 2026 (the **SPA**);
2. the Disclosure Schedule;
3. the IP Assignment Agreement with Brouloul Farmstead IP Holdings, LLC;
4. the September 14, 2026 Letter of Intent (the **LOI**);
5. the Subordinated Promissory Note (the **Seller Note**);
6. the Transition Services Agreement (the **TSA**);
7. the closing logistics email thread; and
8. Lepund's November 4 board resolutions.

I found **five substantive issues** that cut against Lepund. Three affect the SPA's risk allocation. Two sit in the TSA. Several issues only appear when two documents are read together.

**Order of precedence.** SPA Section 11.9 provides that **each Ancillary Agreement (the Seller Note, the IP Assignment Agreement and the TSA) controls as to its subject matter; otherwise the SPA controls.** As a result, the SPA cannot fix defects in the IP Assignment Agreement or the TSA.

**Signing status.** The email thread (Nov. 12) says the SPA "is signed." If so, Issues 1 and 3 require a written SPA amendment under Section 11.3. Issues 2, 4 and 5 can still be fixed in the ancillary agreements before they are executed at the December 1 Closing. In either case, all five should be resolved before Closing.

| # | Issue | Location | Severity |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ridgeview nitrate contamination falls back under the $4,620,000 Cap | SPA §§ 1.1, 9.2(c), 9.5(a), 9.5(c); Disclosure Schedule 4.17 Parts A/B | High |
| 2 | IP Assignment conveys only fluid-milk IP; yogurt, butter and cheese IP stays with Seller's affiliate | SPA §§ 1.1, 4.12, 11.9; IP Assignment § 1.1 and Schedule A | High |
| 3 | Pre-Closing Taxes indemnity expires 18 months after Closing | SPA § 9.1(b); Seller Note § 1.3 | High |
| 4 | Buyer gives an uncapped indemnity to Seller covering Seller's own negligence | TSA §§ 8.1, 8.2, 8.4 | High |
| 5 | Seller may assign or delegate the TSA to anyone, including a competitor | TSA § 12.3 | Medium–High |

The email thread and board resolutions raise no independent issues. I comment on their relevance in Part III.

---

## II. Issues

### Issue 1: The environmental cap carve-out does not reach the Ridgeview nitrate contamination

**Where it appears:**
- SPA Section 1.1 (definition of "Pre-Closing Environmental Liabilities")
- SPA Section 9.2(c) (environmental indemnity)
- SPA Section 9.5(a) (Cap)
- SPA Section 9.5(c) (carve-out)
- Disclosure Schedule, Schedule 4.17, Parts A and B

**The problem:**

- **The indemnity.** Section 9.2(c) has Seller indemnify Buyer for liabilities under Environmental Law, and for Hazardous Materials, arising from pre-Closing operation of the Farms or the Plant.
- **The Cap.** Section 9.5(a) subjects Losses under Sections 9.2(a) **and 9.2(c)** to the Cap. The Cap is **10% of the Purchase Price, or $4,620,000**.
- **The carve-out.** Section 9.5(c) says that Losses arising from "Pre-Closing Environmental Liabilities" "shall not be subject to the Cap." Read alone, this looks protective.
- **The definition.** Section 1.1 defines "Pre-Closing Environmental Liabilities" narrowly. It covers only "the environmental conditions and matters set forth in **Part B of Schedule 4.17**."
- **The schedule.** Part B of Schedule 4.17 ("Remediation Matters") lists only the Hollis Farm decommissioned manure pond, with an estimated closure cost of $640,000. The **Ridgeview Farm groundwater nitrate contamination** appears only in **Part A**, as a "Disclosed Environmental Matter."

**The result:** As drafted, Ridgeview is not a Pre-Closing Environmental Liability. Recovery for it under Section 9.2(c) remains subject to the $4,620,000 Cap.

**Why it matters for Lepund:**

- **Size of the exposure.** The Ridgeview Phase II Report (Aug. 18, 2026) estimates remediation and long-term monitoring at **$3.4 million to $7.8 million**. At the high end, Lepund would bear about **$3.18 million** above the Cap.
- **The Cap is shared.** It is an aggregate cap across Sections 9.2(a) and 9.2(c). Every dollar of Ridgeview cost therefore reduces what Lepund can recover for breaches of general representations, and the reverse is also true. In practice, Lepund's general representation protection could be wiped out.
- **The exposure is live.** Vermont ANR/DEC issued a Notice of Groundwater Exceedance on September 29, 2026. A corrective action work plan is due **January 31, 2027**, which is weeks after Closing.
- **This departs from the deal terms.** LOI Section 5.3 records that "pre-closing environmental liabilities, including Ridgeview Farm nitrate contamination, not subject to the general cap."
- **Disclosure undercuts the representation claim.** Ridgeview is disclosed against Section 4.17. Lepund therefore has no clean breach-of-representation claim and must rely on Section 9.2(c).

**Recommended fix:**

1. Amend the Section 1.1 definition to read: "all liabilities and Losses described in Section 9.2(c), **including the matters set forth in Parts A and B of Schedule 4.17 (expressly including the Ridgeview Farm groundwater nitrate contamination described in the Ridgeview Phase II Report and the Notice of Groundwater Exceedance dated September 29, 2026)**."
2. Alternatively, and at a minimum, move the Ridgeview item into Part B of Schedule 4.17. The better approach is to delete the Part B cross-reference entirely, so that all Section 9.2(c) Losses are uncapped. That matches the LOI.
3. Conform Section 9.5(a) so that the Cap applies only to Section 9.2(a).
4. Consider a dedicated environmental escrow, or a holdback sized to the $7.8 million high estimate. The Seller Note set-off ($6 million, maturing at 18 months) cannot secure a six-year environmental indemnity. Also consider giving Buyer control of the ANR corrective action process, subject to Seller cost-sharing.

---

### Issue 2: The IP Assignment Agreement conveys only fluid-milk IP; yogurt, butter and cheese IP stays with Seller's affiliate

**Where it appears:**
- SPA Section 1.1 (definitions of "Business" and "Assigned IP")
- SPA Section 4.12
- SPA Section 11.9
- IP Assignment Agreement Section 1.1 (definitions of "Business" and "Assigned IP") and Schedule A

**The problem:**

- **The SPA definition.** SPA Section 1.1 defines "Business" as the production, processing, marketing and sale of **organic fluid milk, yogurt, butter and cheese**.
- **The IP Assignment definitions.** IP Assignment Section 1.1 separately defines "Business" as "the **production, processing and sale of organic fluid milk**." It then defines "Assigned IP," including the Trademarks, Recipes and Know-How, and Starter Cultures, as IP "used or held for use in the Business."
- **Which definition governs.** The IP Assignment Agreement uses its own definition rather than borrowing the SPA's; its Section 1.2 imports SPA terms only where they are not defined. Under SPA Section 11.9, the IP Assignment Agreement controls as to its subject matter. **The narrower fluid-milk definition therefore governs what is conveyed.**
- **No backstop in the SPA.** SPA Section 4.12 warrants only that the Company will own the "Assigned IP," which is the term defined in the IP Assignment Agreement. Seller has therefore given no representation that the Company will own all IP needed to run the full Business.
- **Schedule A confirms the gap.** It lists only Class 29 *milk* registrations: KETTLEBROOK ORGANIC (word and design) and RIDGEVIEW PASTURE MILK. It does not list the "Brouloul Farmstead" cheese brand.

**Why it matters for Lepund:**

The following would stay with Brouloul Farmstead IP Holdings, LLC:
- the **yogurt recipes**;
- the **proprietary starter cultures**, which are essential to yogurt and cheese production;
- butter and cheese know-how; and
- the **"Brouloul Farmstead" cheese brand**.

The consequences are serious:
- **The deal premise.** LOI Section 3 identified these specific assets ("Brouloul Farmstead" brand, yogurt and cheese recipes, proprietary starter cultures) as being transferred. The board resolutions (Section 2.4(f)) approved the deal on that basis.
- **Customer contracts.** Material Contracts depend on yogurt and cheese production. These include the Northeast Natural Grocers private-label yogurt agreement, which is itself a closing condition, and the Stonewall drinkable-yogurt co-pack.
- **Non-compete protection is weak.** Seller's affiliate could license the retained cultures and recipes to third parties. The Section 6.5 non-compete limits competition only within five states.
- **Lepund would be paying full price for less than it bargained for.** It would also have no indemnity claim, because Section 4.12 would be accurate as written.

**Recommended fix:**

1. Conform the IP Assignment Agreement's "Business" definition to the SPA's, so it reads "organic fluid milk, yogurt, butter and cheese." Alternatively, define "Business" by cross-reference to the SPA.
2. Add a schedule that expressly lists the Assigned IP, including:
   - the "Brouloul Farmstead" mark and any registrations or applications for it;
   - all yogurt, butter and cheese recipes; and
   - all starter culture strains, with master stock identifiers.
3. Expand Schedule A to cover all registered marks used in any product line.
4. Add an SPA representation (Section 4.12) that the Company will own or have valid rights to **all** IP necessary to conduct the Business as currently conducted. Consider making it a Fundamental Representation, or at least carving it out of the Cap.
5. Confirm that IP Assignment Sections 3.2 (delivery of starter culture stocks; no retained samples) and 5.3 (confidentiality) apply to the yogurt and cheese cultures once they are included.

---

### Issue 3: The Pre-Closing Taxes indemnity expires 18 months after Closing

**Where it appears:**
- SPA Section 9.1(b)
- Seller Note Section 1.3 (Maturity Date)

**The problem:**

- **The survival provision.** SPA Section 9.1(b) provides that Seller's Pre-Closing Taxes indemnity under Section 9.2(b) survives "until the Maturity Date (as defined in the Seller Note)."
- **The Maturity Date.** Seller Note Section 1.3 sets that date at **eighteen (18) months after the Issue Date (the Closing Date)**. With Closing on December 1, 2026, the tax indemnity would expire around **June 1, 2028**.
- **Each document looks reasonable alone.** Linking tax survival to the note might appear designed to align with the set-off right. Read together, however, the two provisions cut Lepund's tax protection to 18 months.

**Why it matters for Lepund:**

- **The limitations period is longer.** Federal and most state assessment periods run at least three years from filing, and longer for substantial understatements. For example, the Company's 2026 return, filed in 2027, stays open into 2030 or later. Pre-Closing tax exposures for 2024 through 2026 would therefore surface after the indemnity has lapsed.
- **No backstop.** The Section 4.14 tax representation is not a Fundamental Representation. It survives only **15 months** under Section 9.1(a), which is even shorter. It is also subject to the Deductible and the Cap.
- **Departure from the deal terms.** LOI Section 5.2 records agreed survival of **60 days after expiration of the applicable statute of limitations**.
- **Buyer bears the cost.** Lepund (through the Company) would bear the cost of Seller-period taxes, even though Seller prepares the pre-Closing income tax returns under Section 7.1.

**Recommended fix:**

1. Amend Section 9.1(b) so that Seller's Section 9.2(b) obligations "survive until sixty (60) days after the expiration of the applicable statute of limitations (giving effect to any waiver or extension thereof)."
2. Add Section 4.14 to the list of Fundamental Representations, or give it the same statute-of-limitations survival period.
3. Remove any implicit link between survival and the Seller Note. The set-off right in Section 9.6 can continue to apply while the note is outstanding, but survival should not depend on it.

---

### Issue 4: Under the TSA, Buyer indemnifies Seller for Seller's own negligence, and that indemnity is uncapped

**Where it appears:**
- TSA Section 8.2 (Indemnification by Recipient)
- TSA Section 8.4 (Limitation of Liability)
- TSA Section 8.1 (for context)

**The problem:**

- **Scope of Buyer's indemnity.** TSA Section 8.2 requires Lepund, as Recipient, to indemnify Seller, as Provider, against all Losses "arising out of or relating to the provision of the Services," "**except to the extent caused by Provider's willful misconduct**." Seller's ordinary and gross negligence are therefore indemnified *by Lepund*.
- **Cap and exclusions.** TSA Section 8.4 caps each party's liability at the total Fees paid. It then provides that the cap and the consequential damages exclusion in Section 8.3 "**shall not apply to Recipient's obligations under Section 8.2**."
- **Seller's indemnity is narrow and capped.** Seller's own indemnity under Section 8.1 covers only gross negligence, willful misconduct and confidentiality breaches. It remains subject to the Fees cap.

**Why it matters for Lepund:**

- **The services are high-risk.** They include raw milk hauling, organic certification support and producer payroll. Examples of Seller negligence that could occur:
  - a contaminated or non-organic load commingled at the Plant;
  - a PMO sanitation lapse leading to a product recall;
  - a recordkeeping failure leading to suspension of organic certification; or
  - a producer pay miscalculation that triggers wage payment claims.
- **The liability runs the wrong way.** In each case, Lepund would owe Seller unlimited indemnity, including consequential losses. Seller's liability to Lepund would be limited to the Fees. Those Fees are modest: about $24,300 per month in fixed fees, plus per-hundredweight hauling.
- **The SPA does not help.** Under SPA Section 11.9, the TSA controls as to its subject matter. The SPA's indemnity structure therefore offers no protection.
- **Insurance does not close the gap.** The Company's recall coverage ($5 million) and Seller's insurance under TSA Section 9 do not address the inverted allocation.

**Recommended fix:**

1. Revise Section 8.2 to exclude Losses "to the extent caused by Provider's (or any Service Personnel's) negligence, gross negligence, willful misconduct, breach of this Agreement or violation of applicable law." Limit Buyer's indemnity to third-party claims arising from Recipient's own use of the Services.
2. Delete the Section 8.4 carve-out for Section 8.2. Buyer's indemnity should be subject to the same cap as Provider's, and to the Section 8.3 exclusion.
3. Broaden Section 8.1 so that Provider indemnifies for its negligence and breach of the Service Standard. Carve Provider's indemnity for food safety, organic certification and confidentiality breaches out of the Fees cap, or set a meaningful fixed cap for those items, such as the recall policy limit.
4. Require Seller to name Lepund and the Company as additional insureds on Seller's general liability, auto and cargo policies.

---

### Issue 5: Seller may assign or delegate the TSA to anyone, including a competitor

**Where it appears:**
- TSA Section 12.3 (Assignment)
- TSA Sections 1.1 ("Company Data") and 5.1 (for context)

**The problem:**

- **One-sided consent rights.** TSA Section 12.3 bars Lepund from assigning without Provider's consent, apart from transfers to Affiliates. By contrast, "**Provider may assign this Agreement, in whole or in part, or delegate the performance of any Service to any Person upon written notice to Recipient and without the consent of Recipient**."
- **No competitor restriction.** Nothing prevents assignment to a competitor.
- **The data at stake.** Under TSA Section 5.1, Provider receives access to the Company's producer pay prices, milk supply contracts, herd records and customer orders. "Company Data" also includes component test results, organic system plans and payroll records.

**Why it matters for Lepund:**

- **Competitor access.** A competing organic dairy processor could take over hauling or producer payroll during the 9-month Term. It would then gain the Company's producer pricing and customer information. This data is exactly what such a competitor would need to poach the Company's independent organic producers, whose supply is scarce, or its customers.
- **Confidentiality protection is incomplete.** TSA Section 7 and SPA Section 6.4 bind Seller and its Affiliates. They do not address the commercial harm of a competitor legitimately holding the data as a service provider.
- **The SPA does not help.** SPA Section 11.4 restricts assignment of the SPA only. Under Section 11.9, the TSA controls as to its subject matter.
- **Service quality risk.** Delegation to an unvetted hauler also threatens organic and PMO compliance.
- **Inconsistent with the LOI.** LOI Section 6 contemplated customary data protection for producer, pricing and customer information.

**Recommended fix:**

1. Revise Section 12.3 so that Provider may not assign the Agreement, or delegate or subcontract any Service, without **Recipient's prior written consent**. Permit transfers only to wholly owned Affiliates of Provider, with Provider remaining liable.
2. Add an express prohibition on any assignment, delegation or subcontracting to a Person (or Affiliate of a Person) that engages in the production, processing or sale of organic dairy products, or that purchases raw organic milk, in the Northeast.
3. Treat a change of control of Provider as an assignment.
4. Give Recipient the right to terminate any Service immediately, without penalty, if a prohibited transfer occurs. Require any approved subcontractor to sign confidentiality terms enforceable directly by the Company.

---

## III. Other Observations

- **Board resolutions (D8).** The November 4 resolutions approve the documents "substantially in the form presented," with changes the Authorized Officer may approve. The fixes above are favorable to Lepund and fall within that authority. No further board action appears necessary. However, Section 2.4(f) shows the board understood that recipes and starter cultures would be transferred, which reinforces Issue 2.
- **Email thread (D7).**
  - The email thread raises no independent legal issue.
  - Note that the short-form trademark assignment Priya circulated covers only the Schedule A milk registrations. It should be expanded once Issue 2 is fixed.
  - The December 1 Closing target leaves limited time. Amendments for Issues 1 and 3, and revised ancillary forms for Issues 2, 4 and 5, should go to Ferrisdale & Moore immediately.
- **Seller Note security.** Even after these fixes, the $6 million note matures at 18 months. That limits Lepund's practical security for longer-tail environmental and tax claims. Consider extending the maturity, or adding an escrow for the environmental indemnity.

---

## IV. Recommended Next Steps

1. Send Seller's counsel a markup covering:
   - an SPA amendment for Issues 1 and 3 (if the SPA is in fact signed);
   - a revised IP Assignment Agreement and schedules (Issue 2); and
   - a revised TSA (Issues 4 and 5).
2. Cite LOI Sections 3, 5.2, 5.3 and 6 as the agreed deal terms for Issues 1, 2 and 3 and the data protection point.
3. Make execution of the conformed IP Assignment Agreement and TSA a condition to Lepund's closing deliveries.
4. Confirm with the client before Closing whether it wants an environmental escrow sized to the Ridgeview high estimate.

Please let me know if you would like me to prepare the markups.

# MEMORANDUM

**TO:** Supervising Partner
**FROM:** [Associate]
**DATE:** November 18, 2026
**RE:** Project Curd: Lepund Creamery Holdings, Inc. acquisition of Kettlebrook Organic Creamery, Inc. Buyer-side issues in the transaction documents

---

## I. Summary

I reviewed all eight documents in the folder:

- the Stock Purchase Agreement dated November 6, 2026 (SPA)
- the Disclosure Schedule
- the IP Assignment Agreement with Brouloul Farmstead IP Holdings, LLC
- the September 14, 2026 Letter of Intent (LOI)
- the Subordinated Promissory Note (Seller Note)
- the Transition Services Agreement (TSA)
- the closing logistics email thread
- Lepund's November 4, 2026 board resolutions

I found four substantive issues that put Lepund at material risk. Each arises from how two or more provisions or documents interact. Three of them depart from terms agreed in the LOI or from the commercial deal described in it.

1. **Environmental cap carve-out misses Ridgeview.** The largest known environmental exposure, the Ridgeview Farm nitrate contamination (up to $7.8 million estimated), falls inside the $4,620,000 Cap. The LOI agreed it would be uncapped.
2. **IP assignment covers fluid milk only.** The yogurt, butter and cheese IP is not conveyed to the Company.
3. **Tax indemnity expires at 18 months.** The Pre-Closing Taxes indemnity ends 18 months after Closing, well before the tax statutes of limitations run. The LOI agreed it would last until 60 days after the statute of limitations expires.
4. **TSA indemnity favors Seller.** The TSA requires Lepund to indemnify Seller, without limit, for Seller's own negligent performance. Seller's liability to Lepund remains capped at the TSA fees.

Two framing points apply throughout:

- **SPA Section 11.9 gives the ancillary agreements priority.** It provides that "[e]ach Ancillary Agreement controls as to its subject matter; otherwise this Agreement controls." The Ancillary Agreements are the Seller Note, the IP Assignment Agreement and the TSA. The SPA therefore cannot be used to fix problems in those documents. Each ancillary agreement must be corrected on its own terms.
- **The SPA may already be signed.** The SPA is dated November 6, 2026, and Dana Whitcomb's November 12 email says "[n]ow that the SPA is signed." If that is right, Issues 1 and 3 will need a written amendment under SPA Section 11.3 rather than a markup. The IP Assignment Agreement, Seller Note and TSA are to be signed at Closing, targeted for December 1, 2026, so they can still be revised before execution. We should confirm the SPA's status right away.

The email thread and the board resolutions are logistical and approval documents. Neither raises a substantive issue. I note one related point on the resolutions in Part III.

---

## II. Issues

### Issue 1: Ridgeview nitrate contamination is not covered by the environmental cap carve-out

**Where it appears**
- SPA Section 1.1, definition of "Pre-Closing Environmental Liabilities"
- SPA Sections 9.2(c), 9.5(a) and 9.5(c)
- Disclosure Schedule, Schedule 4.17, Parts A and B
- Compare LOI Section 5.3

**The problem**

Each provision looks protective on its own. The problem appears only when they are read together.

- **The indemnity.** SPA Section 9.2(c) requires Seller to indemnify Lepund for all liabilities under Environmental Law arising from pre-Closing ownership or operation of the Farms or the Plant.
- **The Cap.** Section 9.5(a) subjects Losses under Sections 9.2(a) and 9.2(c) to the Cap. The Cap is 10% of the Purchase Price, or **$4,620,000**.
- **The carve-out.** Section 9.5(c) provides that Losses arising from "Pre-Closing Environmental Liabilities ... shall not be subject to the Cap or the Deductible."
- **The definition.** Section 1.1 defines "Pre-Closing Environmental Liabilities" narrowly. It covers only "the environmental conditions and matters set forth in **Part B of Schedule 4.17**."
- **The schedule.** Part B of Schedule 4.17 ("Remediation Matters") lists only one item: the decommissioned manure storage pond at Hollis Farm, with an estimated closure cost of $640,000. The Ridgeview Farm groundwater nitrate contamination appears in **Part A** ("Disclosed Environmental Matters"), together with two minor, resolved items.

The Ridgeview contamination is therefore not a "Pre-Closing Environmental Liability" as defined. Lepund's recovery for it under Section 9.2(c) stays subject to the $4,620,000 Cap. That Cap is also shared with all general representation and warranty claims under Section 9.2(a).

**Why it matters for Lepund**

- **The exposure exceeds the Cap.** The Ridgeview Phase II Report (August 18, 2026) estimates remediation and long-term monitoring at **$3,400,000 to $7,800,000**. At the high end, Lepund would bear about $3.2 million or more with no recourse.
- **The exposure is live.** Vermont DEC issued a Notice of Groundwater Exceedance on September 29, 2026 and requires a corrective action work plan by January 31, 2027. Remediation costs will begin shortly after Closing.
- **Ridgeview will use up the Cap.** Because the Cap is shared, a large Ridgeview claim could exhaust it and leave nothing for breaches of the operational representations, such as organic certification, food safety and material contracts.
- **The draft departs from the agreed deal.** LOI Section 5.3 states that "pre-closing environmental liabilities, including Ridgeview Farm nitrate contamination, not subject to the general cap." The current drafting reverses that agreed treatment. It also shifts the uncapped protection to the smaller Hollis matter.
- **Disclosure may weaken other claims.** Because Ridgeview is disclosed against Section 4.17, Lepund likely could not bring a separate representation claim for it either.

**Recommended fix**

Amend the SPA Section 1.1 definition to track Section 9.2(c) and the LOI. For example:

> "'Pre-Closing Environmental Liabilities' means any liability under Environmental Law, or any release or presence of Hazardous Materials, arising from the ownership or operation of the Farms or the Plant before the Closing, including the matters set forth in Parts A and B of Schedule 4.17 and, for the avoidance of doubt, the Ridgeview Farm groundwater nitrate contamination described in the Ridgeview Phase II Report."

At a minimum, move the Ridgeview contamination into Part B of Schedule 4.17. The definitional fix is preferable because it also covers conditions not yet discovered.

Lepund should also consider:

- confirming that Seller's indemnity covers the cost of the DEC corrective action work plan and Lepund's control of the remediation process; and
- given the size of the exposure and the 18-month Seller Note, asking for a specific environmental escrow or holdback (see the related point under Issue 3).

If the SPA has been signed, document these changes in a Section 11.3 amendment executed before or at Closing.

---

### Issue 2: The IP Assignment Agreement conveys only fluid milk IP

**Where it appears**
- SPA Section 1.1 (definitions of "Business" and "Assigned IP")
- SPA Sections 4.12 and 11.9
- IP Assignment Agreement Section 1.1 (definitions of "Business" and "Assigned IP") and Schedule A
- Compare LOI Sections 1.2 and 3

**The problem**

The SPA and the IP Assignment Agreement define "Business" differently.

| Document | Definition of "Business" |
|---|---|
| SPA Section 1.1 | "the production, processing, marketing and sale of organic fluid milk, yogurt, butter and cheese" |
| IP Assignment Agreement Section 1.1 | "the production, processing and sale of organic fluid milk" |

Under the IP Assignment Agreement, "Assigned IP" covers only IP "used or held for use in the Business." Each category (Trademarks, Recipes and Know-How, Starter Cultures, Copyrights and domain names) is also limited to items "used in the Business."

- **The narrower definition controls.** Under SPA Section 11.9, the IP Assignment Agreement controls as to its subject matter, so its definition governs what is actually conveyed.
- **The SPA representation gives no fallback.** SPA Section 4.12 represents only that the Company will own the "Assigned IP," and the SPA defines that term by reference to the IP Assignment Agreement.
- **The schedule confirms the gap.** Schedule A lists only marks registered for Class 29 "Milk": KETTLEBROOK ORGANIC (word and design) and RIDGEVIEW PASTURE MILK. It does not list the "Brouloul Farmstead" cheese brand.

**Why it matters for Lepund**

The following would remain with Seller's affiliate:

- the yogurt and cheese recipes;
- the proprietary **starter cultures**; and
- the **"Brouloul Farmstead" cheese brand**.

The LOI (Section 3.1) expressly identifies all of these as IP Lepund was acquiring.

The commercial consequences are serious:

- Yogurt and cheese are core to the Company's revenue. They include the Northeast Natural Grocers private-label yogurt contract, which is a consent-condition customer under SPA Section 8.1(e), the Stonewall drinkable-yogurt co-pack, and cheese-shop customers such as Bayside Specialty Cheese Shops.
- Without the cultures and recipes, the Company may not be able to make those products. Using them after Closing could expose the Company to trade secret claims from the affiliate.
- The IP Assignment Agreement's confidentiality, no-challenge and delivery covenants (Sections 3.2, 5.3 and 5.4) apply only to Assigned IP. The affiliate would therefore have no obligation to hand over culture stocks, keep the recipes confidential or refrain from using them.
- SPA Section 6.5 bars Seller's affiliates from engaging in the "Business," which may limit their own use. It does not transfer ownership, however, and it ends after five years.

**Recommended fix**

1. **Conform the definition.** Revise the definition of "Business" in IP Assignment Agreement Section 1.1 to match the SPA exactly: "production, processing, marketing and sale of organic fluid milk, yogurt, butter and cheese." Alternatively, define it by cross-reference to the SPA definition.
2. **Expand Schedule A.** List all registered and unregistered marks, including BROULOUL FARMSTEAD and any yogurt and cheese marks. Add schedules identifying the specific recipes and starter culture strains, including master and working stocks, to be delivered under Section 3.2.
3. **Broaden SPA Section 4.12.** Add a representation that the Company will own or have valid rights to all IP necessary to conduct the Business as currently conducted (a "sufficiency" representation). This gives Lepund a backstop if any item is left out. As a related point, Section 4.12 is not a Fundamental Representation, so claims under it are subject to the 15-month survival period and the Cap. Consider adding it to the Fundamental Representations.

---

### Issue 3: The Pre-Closing Taxes indemnity expires with the Seller Note, 18 months after Closing

**Where it appears**
- SPA Section 9.1(b)
- Seller Note Section 1.3
- Related: SPA Sections 4.14, 9.1(a) and 9.6
- Compare LOI Section 5.2

**The problem**

- **The survival clause.** SPA Section 9.1(b) provides that Seller's obligations under Section 9.2(b), which covers Pre-Closing Taxes, "shall survive until the Maturity Date (as defined in the Seller Note)." On its own, this reads as a sensible link to Lepund's set-off security.
- **The Maturity Date.** Seller Note Section 1.3 sets the Maturity Date at "eighteen (18) months after the Issue Date (the Closing Date)." On its own, that is ordinary payment drafting.

Read together, the two provisions mean the Pre-Closing Taxes indemnity ends **18 months after Closing**. Under SPA Section 9.1(c), no claim may be brought after that date unless it was asserted in writing beforehand.

**Why it matters for Lepund**

- **Tax authorities have more time than Lepund does.** Federal and state taxing authorities can generally assess for at least three years after a return is filed, and longer in some cases. Kettlebrook's 2024, 2025 and 2026 returns, including the short period ending on the Closing Date, will remain open to audit long after the indemnity has expired. Lepund, as the Company's owner, would bear any pre-Closing deficiency, interest and penalties.
- **The tax representation is no backstop.** The Section 4.14 tax representation is a general representation. It is not among the Fundamental Representations, which are Sections 4.1, 4.2, 4.3 and 4.20. It therefore survives only **15 months** under Section 9.1(a), which is even shorter, and it is subject to the Deductible and the Cap.
- **Lepund's set-off right ends at the same time.** Set-off is available only against amounts "then due or thereafter becoming due" under the Seller Note (SPA Section 9.6; Seller Note Section 5.1). Once the note is paid at maturity, Lepund has no security for later tax claims or for the six-year environmental indemnity.
- **The draft departs from the agreed deal.** LOI Section 5.2 provides that the tax indemnity "would survive until 60 days after expiration of the applicable statute of limitations." The current drafting ties survival to a payment date that has nothing to do with tax exposure.

**Recommended fix**

Amend SPA Section 9.1(b) to read:

> "The obligations of Seller under Section 9.2(b) shall survive until sixty (60) days after the expiration of the applicable statute of limitations (giving effect to any waiver, mitigation or extension thereof)."

This brings the provision in line with the LOI and with the survival period already used for Fundamental Representations.

Lepund should also consider:

- adding Section 4.14 to the Fundamental Representations, or carving tax matters out of the 15-month period; and
- negotiating a tax and environmental escrow, or extending the Seller Note, so that Lepund keeps security beyond 18 months.

If the SPA has been signed, document this in a Section 11.3 amendment. Do not change the Seller Note's Maturity Date as the means of fixing this, because that would alter the economic terms the board approved.

### Issue 4: Lepund indemnifies Seller for Seller's own negligence under the TSA, with no cap

**Where it appears**
- TSA Sections 8.1, 8.2, 8.3 and 8.4
- Related: SPA Section 11.9

**The problem**

- **Lepund's indemnity is almost unlimited in scope.** TSA Section 8.2 requires Lepund, as Recipient, to indemnify Seller, as Provider, and its affiliates and Service Personnel against "all Losses arising out of or relating to the provision of the Services ... except to the extent caused by Provider's willful misconduct." The only exclusion is willful misconduct, so Lepund indemnifies Seller for Seller's **ordinary negligence and even its gross negligence** in performing the Services.
- **Lepund's indemnity has no ceiling.** Section 8.4 caps "each party's" aggregate liability at the total Fees paid, but then states that the limitations in Sections 8.3 and 8.4 "**shall not apply to Recipient's obligations under Section 8.2**." Lepund's indemnity is therefore both uncapped and not subject to the consequential damages exclusion.
- **Seller's exposure is narrow and capped.** Seller's indemnity to Lepund under Section 8.1 covers only gross negligence, willful misconduct and confidentiality breaches. Its overall liability is capped at TSA fees. Those fees are cost-based and modest: roughly $14,500 per month for certification support and $9,800 per month for payroll, plus hauling at $1.42 to $1.68 per hundredweight.
- **The two indemnities overlap.** For Seller's gross negligence, Seller must indemnify Lepund under Section 8.1, while Lepund must indemnify Seller for the same Losses under Section 8.2. The result is, at best, circular and, at worst, a complete wash in Seller's favor.

**Why it matters for Lepund**

The TSA services are high-risk:

- **Milk hauling.** A mishandled load could contaminate the supply, for example through a non-dedicated or improperly sanitized tanker or commingling with non-organic milk.
- **Organic certification support.** Lapsed pasture logs or inaccurate organic system plans could lead to suspension or revocation of certification.
- **Producer payroll.** Errors could violate wage payment law or trigger claims from producers.

Losses from any of these, such as a product recall, loss of organic premium, third-party claims or regulatory penalties, could far exceed TSA fees. Lepund would have to reimburse Seller for those Losses without limit, even though Seller caused them. Seller would have little incentive to perform carefully during the 9-month Term.

Because the TSA controls as to its subject matter under SPA Section 11.9, the SPA's indemnity and cap structure would not override these terms. The Company's own Product Contamination and Recall policy ($5 million) would be eroded by losses that Seller should bear.

**Recommended fix**

- **Section 8.2.** Narrow Lepund's indemnity to Losses arising from Lepund's own breach, negligence or willful misconduct. At a minimum, revise the exception to read "except to the extent caused by Provider's (or any Service Personnel's) breach of this Agreement, negligence, gross negligence or willful misconduct."
- **Section 8.4.** Delete the carve-out for Recipient's Section 8.2 obligations so the indemnity is subject to the cap and to the Section 8.3 consequential damages exclusion, on a mutual basis. If Seller insists on any uncapped indemnity, it should be reciprocal.
- **Section 8.1.** Expand Seller's indemnity to cover Losses from Provider's negligence, breach of the Service Standard in Section 4.1 or violation of law. Carve those Losses, along with confidentiality breaches and Provider's gross negligence and willful misconduct, out of the Section 8.4 cap. A cap set at fees is far too low against recall and certification-loss exposure. If a cap remains, set it at a meaningful fixed amount rather than fees paid.
- **Section 9 (insurance).** Require Lepund and the Company to be named as additional insureds on Provider's general liability, auto and cargo policies, with a waiver of subrogation.
